title: MB9-05582
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow. XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti, and XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Brazil.

Ms. XXXX was raped and threatened with death in Haiti in 2011. She left Haiti for the XXXX XXXX and later travelled to Brazil that same year. She left Brazil in XXXX 2016 due to the violence against Haitians in Brazil, including the death of one of her childhood friends. She arrived in the United States in XXXX 2016 and then made her way to Canada where she arrived in XXXX 2017. Ms. XXXX fears that she would be the victim of criminality or gender-based violence if she returned to Haiti. She fears that she and her son would be mistreated, seriously harmed or killed if they returned to Brazil.

The RPD concluded that Ms. XXXX was excluded from protection under Article 1E of the refugee Convention and s. 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It found that Ms. XXXX had permanent resident status in Brazil but lost it because she remained outside of Brazil for more than two years. However, the RPD found that Ms. XXXX could obtain a residence visa which would allow her to return to Brazil because her son is a citizen of that country. As well, the RPD found that the evidence did not establish that, if they returned to Brazil, either Ms. XXXX or her son would face a serious risk of persecution or the likelihood of any of the kinds of serious harm that would make them persons in need of protection.

For the reasons set out below, the appeal is denied. I do not agree with any of the reasons provided by the Appellants as to why they believe the RPD erred in concluding that Ms. XXXX is excluded from protection under Article 1E of the Convention and s. 98 of IRPA. I also agree with the RPD's conclusion that the evidence does not establish that Ms. XXXX son would face a serious risk of persecution or the likelihood of serious harm in Brazil.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1

I note at the outset that the Appellants do not contest that Ms. XXXX had permanent resident status in Brazil but lost it due to her being outside the country for over two years. The Appellants also do not contest that Ms. XXXX would be able to obtain permanent resident status in Brazil due to her son's Brazilian citizenship. The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to properly assess Ms. XXXX fear of persecution for herself and her son if they return to Brazil as part of whether their departure was voluntary. RPD did not err in assessment of risk that the Appellants would face in Brazil
I do not agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellants failed to establish that they faced a serious possibility of persecution in Brazil.

When asked about her fear in Brazil, Ms. XXXX said that Brazilians had started to kill Haitians in 2015, including a childhood friend of hers.2 She also said that she read on Facebook and YouTube about Haitians being killed by Brazilians. When the RPD asked her whether she herself had any problems in Brazil, she twice said no.3 Likewise when Ms. XXXX counsel asked her whether she herself had any problems in Brazil, she said no. When her counsel asked her how Brazilians treated her, she testified that she had been insulted on the streets on almost a daily basis and isolated at work as Brazilian colleagues did not sit with the Haitian workers.4 She also said that Brazilians treated Haitians with contempt in places like public transit. When asked whether she had had problems in shops, she said she had not because she would have been able to make a complaint and the employee would have been dismissed. She also indicated that her son had not had any problems in his day care.5

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in not taking into consideration that Ms. XXXX was raped in Haiti when evaluating her fear in Brazil. I do not agree. Even if Ms. XXXX was raped in Haiti in 2011, I do not agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in failing to consider this factor in its assessment of the risk of persecution or serious harm that she faced in Brazil. While it is unfortunate that Ms. XXXX went through the experience of being raped in 2011 in Haiti, the incident is not a relevant consideration for assessing Ms. XXXX risk in Brazil since the perpetrator of the rape was an unknown person and it took place in Haiti. There was no suggestion whatsoever that the perpetrator may be in Brazil or that he would pose any risk to Ms. XXXX in Brazil.

I also find that the RPD was correct in finding that any racism or racial discrimination that the Appellants experienced, or might experience in the future in Brazil, did not rise to the level of persecution.

I agree with the RPD that the experiences described by Ms. XXXX do not amount to persecution, even when read in the context of the information on racial discrimination contained in the NDP for Brazil and considered cumulatively. The Appellants do not make any argument for how the RPD erred except to note that the RPD had itself acknowledged that the objective evidence supports the existence of racism against Haitians in Brazil. I do not find that this was an error. Not all discrimination amounts to persecution. In order for discrimination against a person to amount to persecution, it must be serious and occur with repetition. It must also have consequences of a prejudicial nature for the person, such as when an individual is denied a core human right, such as the right to practice religion or to earn a livelihood.6 I do not agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in referring to the existence of racism while also finding that they had not established a serious possibility of persecution. I note that Ms. XXXX was able to earn a livelihood in Brazil as she was employed for the two-year period up to the time she left Brazil. Her husband was also employed in Brazil. While she did describe racist attitudes to which she was subject in public and at work, I agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX own testimony in which she responded three times that she did not personally have problems in Brazil would suggest that these attitudes and actions did not rise to the level of causing problems for her, let alone amount to persecution.

The Appellants also seem to suggest that the RPD erred in failing to refer to a key piece of evidence without clearly saying what this piece of evidence was. I do not see any key piece of evidence arising from Ms. XXXX Basis of Claim form or her testimony that was not referred to and taking into consideration by the RPD in its very thorough analysis of her evidence.

I also do not agree with the Appellants that it is relevant that the NDP speaks to a generalized climate of violence and criminality in Brazil. Such a generalized level of criminality or violence does not, by itself, establish as a serious possibility of persecution or the likelihood of the kind of harm necessary to establish that a claimant is a person in need of protection.7 I note that Ms. XXXX did testify that her cousin was killed in front of her, in her view due to the fact that he was Haitian. While this death was no doubt difficult for Ms. XXXX, the RPD was correct to find that, even when considered against the evidence in the NDP for Brazil about the disproportionate level of violence against Afro-Brazilians, this death did not establish a serious possibility that the Appellants would be persecuted or a likelihood that they would be subjected to serious harm if they returned to Brazil.

Finally, I do not agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in not properly considering the documentary evidence regarding the participation of police in many incidents of violence in Brazil, especially against Afro-Brazilians. To begin, Ms. XXXX did not make any allegation of violence at the hands of the police. In my view, the objective documentation on police violence in the NDP for Brazil, on its own, is insufficient to establish that the Appellants would face a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of any of the kinds of harm that would make them persons in need of protection in Brazil.

For the above reasons, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
